A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoRefine despite the revised subtitle. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering.

before.justification: v3 reports original AutoRefine evaluations on seven QA benchmarks, component ablations, model-size comparisons, search-behavior analyses, and appendix training dynamics and case studies.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds external-refiner comparisons, repeated-run statistics, reward-design experiments, and an analysis of complex answers.

M1.justification: Appendices C.3–C.4 introduce evaluated AutoRefine reward variants: linear reward combinations, rewards on retrieved documents, and token- or word-level recall replacing binary CEM. These are limited training-objective alternatives; the default search/refine loop, piecewise reward, prompt, and GRPO objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The NQ/HotpotQA training mixture and seven QA benchmarks remain unchanged. Appendix C.4 adds a separately evaluated population with answers longer than five words, drawn from TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and Musique. This adds focused answer-complexity coverage without introducing new datasets.

E2.justification: Section 3.4.3 and Table 4 add a substantive comparator family: Search-R1 augmented with BART or Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct refiners, with Qwen tested for summarization alone and summarization plus planning. These directly challenge whether external summarization can substitute for learned refinement. The original Table 1 comparators remain.

E3.justification: New experiments vary external-refiner prompting, retrieval-reward targets and combinations, and evaluate the greater-than-five-word answer subset. Existing benchmark splits, Wikipedia corpus, retrieval settings, and training specifications are retained. The 3B/7B and EM/F1/CEM evaluations already appeared in v3.

E4.justification: v4 adds substantial diagnostic studies of learned versus external refinement, document versus refinement rewards, linear versus nonlinear reward combinations, and reward granularity for complex answers. These extend v3's component and retrieval-depth ablations. Existing training dynamics and both appendix cases are retained, although the first case's initial AutoRefine query is revised.

E5.justification: Unlike v3's point-estimate comparison tables, Appendix C.2/Table 7 reports three runs with different random seeds, means and standard deviations for AutoRefine, ReSearch, and Search-R1, and t-test p-values of 5.49e-6 and 2.85e-6 against the respective baselines. This newly documents uncertainty; v3's run count was unspecified.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their scores, while Tables 4 and 7–9 add substantial results. Table 4 reports averages of 0.317, 0.328, and 0.301 for the three external refiners versus AutoRefine's 0.405. Table 9 reports complex-answer averages of 0.177 with CEM and 0.216 with word recall. Table 8 also introduces an inconsistency: its answer-only average is 0.371 despite identical per-dataset scores yielding 0.376 in Table 2.

T1.justification: The task formulation and Equations (1)–(4) remain unchanged. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or derivation is added. The new reward experiments use standard recall measures and linear combinations without developing new mathematical arguments.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contribution claims remain the same: explicit refinement during retrieval-augmented reasoning, retrieval-specific rewards, and improved QA performance, including the retained 6.9% claim. The revised subtitle and additional evidence do not redefine the overarching contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations distinguishing learned refinement from summarization, hypothesizes why nonlinear rewards prioritize final answers, and identifies a weakness of CEM rewards on complex answers. It also removes the inaccurate 3B-only limitation and updates the EM-only qualification to include F1; v3 already contained 7B and additional-metric results.

D1.justification: The new experiments specify external-refiner backbones and prompting modes and describe operational reward alternatives. This provides limited additional implementation information, although exact refiner prompts and complex-answer subset counts are absent. Appendix B's hardware, hyperparameters, software, and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to BART and Jin et al.'s empirical study of reasoning-search agents. The introduction shifts its SFT criticism from poor generalization toward the cost of constructing search trajectories and more accurately describes prior methods as reasoning over retrieved content. Appendix A's broader positioning is retained.

P1.justification: v4 changes the subtitle, locally rewrites the introduction, condenses the model-size/metric discussion, revises limitations and future work, and inserts new experimental subsections. Most existing prose and the overall section hierarchy remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn with different multi-hop examples, and four new tables display external-refiner, statistical, reward-design, and complex-answer results. Existing implementation, dataset, and case-study tables are retained and renumbered. The empirical plots remain unchanged apart from placement.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens empirical scrutiny through direct external-refiner controls, reward-design tests, complex-answer analysis, and three-seed uncertainty reporting. It also removes limitations contradicted by results already present in v3. These benefits improve support for the method and clarify its boundaries. However, sparse specifications for the new experiments and t-tests limit their evidential strength, while Table 8's inconsistent average and stale Renoir references after Figure 1's redesign introduce local reporting problems.
